Addiction to alcohol

A small three-arm trial found lower short-term craving and AUDIT scores with tPBM or combined tPBM plus taVNS than with taVNS alone. Participants had subclinical alcohol use, and the older uncontrolled study did not measure abstinence or relapse.

Publications and records

2direct human publications

Publication and study types

Human RCT: 1 (n=60 randomized; 58 completed and analyzed; three-arm active comparator)

Human non-randomized study: 1 (n=53; single-arm laser plus auricular acupuncture)

Mapped animal: 1 mouse study of alcohol-related cognition, not addiction treatment

Systematic reviews: 0

Meta-analyses: 0

In-vitro studies: 0

Ex-vivo studies: 0

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Craving response — Kwon et al. defined response as a ≥30% reduction in PACS. Adjusted odds were higher with tPBM than taVNS alone (OR 8.09, 95% CI 1.81–36.10; p=0.006); 58 participants were analyzed, so the estimate is imprecise (Kwon et al., 2026).

Craving score — the three-group ANCOVA found a group effect (F(2,54)=5.24; p=0.008). Both tPBM and combined tPBM+taVNS had lower AUDIT scores than taVNS alone (p≤0.011).

Drinking-behavior response — the reported odds ratio was 16.73 for combined tPBM+taVNS versus taVNS alone. This estimate applies to the combination arm, not PBM alone, and comes from small groups.

The 2004 uncontrolled combined-treatment study reported mood and beta-endorphin changes, not abstinence, consumption, or relapse estimates.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for short-term craving and AUDIT-score changes in subclinical alcohol use

Very low for treatment of alcohol use disorder or relapse prevention

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small three-arm trial found lower short-term craving and AUDIT scores with tPBM or combined tPBM plus taVNS than with taVNS alone. Participants had subclinical alcohol use, and the older uncontrolled study did not measure abstinence or relapse.

Summary of the Evidence

Two human publications directly address alcohol dependence or subclinical alcohol use: one 2026 three-arm randomized active-comparator trial and one 2004 uncontrolled adjunct study. The randomized study assigned 60 participants to tPBM, taVNS, or combined stimulation; 58 completed the intervention and were analyzed. A separate mouse study mapped from alcohol-related cognitive impairment examined learning and brain-tissue outcomes, not addiction treatment. No in-vitro or ex-vivo study directly examining alcohol addiction was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

In 2026, 60 adults with subclinical alcohol use were randomized to home-based tPBM, taVNS, or both for five weeks; 58 participants (20 taVNS, 19 tPBM, and 19 combined) completed and entered the analysis. Both tPBM and combined-treatment groups had lower Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS) and Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) scores than the taVNS-only group. This was an active-comparator study without sham-PBM or usual-care arms, and participants did not meet criteria for alcohol use disorder, so it does not establish efficacy for dependence or relapse prevention (Kwon et al., 2026, PMID 42258987).

An uncontrolled 2004 study followed 53 people with alcohol dependence receiving laser biostimulation alongside laser auricular acupuncture. It reported changes in depressive symptoms and plasma beta-endorphin, but did not establish abstinence, reduced relapse, or a comparative PBM effect. The co-intervention also prevents isolating the contribution of laser biostimulation (Zalewska-Kaszubska and Obzejta, 2004, PMID 15674998).

Animal evidence

A mouse model of adolescent chronic alcohol exposure reported improved cognitive and spatial-memory performance and reduced hippocampal reactive gliosis after PBM. These findings concern alcohol-associated brain changes; the model did not test craving, dependence, withdrawal, or relapse (Hong et al., 2025, PMID 39793712).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell-culture or ex-vivo study directly examining PBM for alcohol addiction was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The Kwon trial used the iSyncMe device (iMediSync Inc., Seoul, Republic of Korea), an 850-nm LED system delivering light to 19 scalp positions. Each 15-minute home session comprised three sequential five-minute phases: parietal/occipital stimulation at 10 Hz, whole-brain stimulation at 15 Hz, and frontal stimulation at 18 Hz. Participants used the device five times weekly for five weeks (25 sessions); the paper did not report a reproducible fluence or irradiance. The older adjunct study used low-energy 514-nm green and 633-nm red laser light at neck and ear points alongside auricular acupuncture; a device model was not verified. The mapped mouse study used 830-nm near-infrared light. These protocols do not establish a shared dose or a treatment schedule for alcohol use disorder.

Interpretation

The controlled human signal is limited to short-term questionnaire outcomes in a small subclinical-use sample compared with taVNS. The older study was uncontrolled and multimodal, while the mouse findings are indirect. No controlled trial has established that PBM reduces alcohol consumption, supports treatment retention, achieves abstinence, or prevents relapse in people with alcohol use disorder.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The randomized study found lower short-term craving and AUDIT scores with tPBM and combined tPBM plus taVNS than with taVNS alone. The sample was small and subclinical, and no sham-PBM or usual-care arm was included. The older uncontrolled study combined laser biostimulation with auricular acupuncture and measured mood and beta-endorphin, not abstinence or relapse. Neither study establishes treatment effects in alcohol use disorder or relapse prevention.
